script.opening: "I’m really worried about Ivy — raging temperature for six days now, Calpol and Nurofen barely touch it. She’s got a blotchy rash, really red eyes but not gunky, cracked red lips, a tongue like a strawberry, and puffy red hands. So miserable. Everyone says it’s just a virus, but six days?"

facts.text: Mother, Jade, on video with Ivy (3) on her lap. Ivy is grizzly, flushed, clingy and won’t settle.
Six days, up to 39.8. Comes down a little with Calpol and Nurofen, then straight back up. Saw the out-of-hours GP on day 2 — "probably viral".

Fever first; red eyes and a blotchy rash on her body two days later; then cracked red lips and a red "strawberry" tongue; hands and feet red and puffy since yesterday. Eyes red but no gunk. Tender lump on the right side of her neck.

Awake but grizzly; responds to Mum, smiles a little at her favourite toy. Drinking less than normal, wet nappy/wee about 3 times today. No cough, no runny nose, breathing normal. Rash blanches when Jade presses a glass. No vomiting or diarrhoea. No fits.
Born at term, healthy. Vaccinations "I think up to date — I’d need to check her red book". No medicines except Calpol/Nurofen. No allergies. Nobody else ill at home. No travel abroad.
Lives with partner, Craig, and baby son (8 months). Jade has a car. Craig is at work but can come home.

Worried, tired, a little defensive because you feel nobody is listening. If the doctor takes you seriously, relief. Ask: "Is it serious?" and "Can I drive her in myself?". Ask what to give for the fever.

ice.ideas: "Everyone says it’s a virus, but I don’t believe that any more."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "I feel something’s really wrong. She’s never been this poorly, and nobody’s listening." She fears she’ll be seen as a fussy mum.
ice.expectations: "Find out what it is. Maybe something stronger for the fever."

cues: "Six days?" — the length of fever is the key red flag.
"Everyone says it’s just a virus" — her instinct has been dismissed.
"Can I drive her in myself?" — practical arrangements for same-day assessment.

checkpoints.text: Recognises possible KAWASAKI — fever lasting 5 days or more (NICE NG143: be aware without needing 4 features) with bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, mucosal changes, cervical lymphadenopathy, polymorphous rash, extremity changes
Knows it is CLINICAL and is alert to INCOMPLETE/ATYPICAL Kawasaki (esp. infants, higher coronary risk) — low referral threshold
Understands the CORONARY ARTERY ANEURYSM complication and that early recognition/treatment reduces risk

Makes an URGENT same-day paediatric referral/admission after an NG143 traffic-light and NG254 sepsis assessment (recognising the limits of video), knowing treatment is IVIG + aspirin within ~10 days, with echocardiography, and that aspirin is not given at home (BNFC)
Considers/excludes mimics (measles, scarlet fever, viral exanthems, toxin-mediated illness) without delaying referral
Takes the prolonged fever and the mother’s concern seriously, validating that 6 days of fever warrants action not more reassurance
Explains the need for urgent paediatric assessment clearly and calmly, checking understanding
Arranges disposition: urgent same-day paediatric referral, deterioration advice en route, clear communication — recognising Kawasaki, not dismissing as "just a virus"

worked.txt: "You’re right to push — six days of high fever that won’t come down, with red eyes, cracked lips and that rash, is NOT something to keep calling a virus. There’s a condition I’m concerned about called Kawasaki disease."

"Can you show me Ivy on the camera — her eyes, lips and tongue, the rash, her hands and feet, and her neck? … She has several features plus the long fever, which is exactly why I want her seen in person today — I can’t check her heart rate, circulation or how dry she is over video. Is she drinking and passing urine? Any breathing difficulty or very sleepy spells?"

"We act fast because, untreated, this can affect the blood vessels around the heart — and treatment within the first ten days or so greatly reduces that risk. That’s why it’s urgent, not wait-and-see."

"I’m referring Ivy to the children’s team to be seen today — they’ll confirm it, do a heart scan, and treat with immunoglobulin and aspirin if it’s Kawasaki. Please don’t give her aspirin yourself — it’s only used by the specialists."
"You did exactly the right thing trusting your instinct and bringing her — this isn’t you overreacting."

"Keep her comfortable and give plenty of fluids. Use Calpol or Nurofen only if she’s distressed, not both at the same time. If she becomes very drowsy, breathless or much worse, call 999. I’ll make sure the team are expecting her."

f.learning: KAWASAKI DISEASE is a medium-vessel vasculitis of young children. NICE NG143: be aware of it in any child with FEVER lasting 5 DAYS or longer — 4 features are not required (the "≥4 of 5" rule is the AHA 2017 research definition, international); the features are bilateral NON-purulent conjunctivitis; mucosal changes (red/cracked lips, strawberry tongue); cervical lymphadenopathy; polymorphous rash; and extremity changes (palm/sole erythema-oedema, later peeling). It is a CLINICAL diagnosis with no single confirmatory test (inflammatory markers and later thrombocytosis support it), and clinicians must be alert to INCOMPLETE/ATYPICAL Kawasaki — especially in INFANTS, who present atypically and are at higher coronary risk — keeping a low referral threshold. The critical reason for early recognition is the risk of CORONARY ARTERY ANEURYSMS (a leading cause of acquired paediatric heart disease), substantially reduced by prompt treatment, so a prolonged-fever child with these features must not be dismissed as "just a virus". The action is an URGENT same-day paediatric referral/admission after an NG143 traffic-light and NICE NG254 sepsis assessment (on video, heart rate, capillary refill and hydration cannot be judged; any red or high-risk feature means emergency transfer): treatment is IV immunoglobulin plus aspirin, ideally within the first ~10 days, with echocardiography — primary care’s role is recognition and urgent referral. Aspirin is a specialist exception to the under-16 rule (BNFC): parents must not give it at home; antipyretics are for distress only and not given together (NG143). Consider and exclude mimics (measles, scarlet fever, other viral exanthems, toxin-mediated illness, drug reactions), but persistent high fever ≥5 days with the mucocutaneous cluster warrants paediatric assessment regardless. Validate the worried parent repeatedly told "it’s just a virus", recognise the pattern, and refer urgently the same day.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG143 (Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management, 2019) · [2] NICE NG254 (Suspected sepsis in under 16s) · [3] Eleftheriou et al., Management of Kawasaki disease, Arch Dis Child 2014;99:74–83 (UK) · [4] American Heart Association scientific statement on Kawasaki disease (McCrindle et al., Circulation 2017, international)
knowledge.summary: Fever lasting five days or more in a young child should make you think of Kawasaki disease. Ivy has the fever plus conjunctival injection, lip and tongue changes, a rash, hand changes and a neck node. She needs the paediatric team today, because early immunoglobulin treatment reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysms.

points.h: Think of it at five days
points.t: NICE NG143 [1]: be aware of the possibility of Kawasaki disease in children with fever that has lasted 5 days or longer. Fever of 5 days or more is also an amber feature in the NG143 traffic-light table. Since 2019 NG143 no longer requires 4 of the 5 principal features before you consider it, because early and incomplete cases often show fewer.

NG143 [1] lists: bilateral conjunctival injection without exudate; erythema and cracking of the lips, strawberry tongue or erythema of the oral and pharyngeal mucosa; oedema and erythema of the hands or feet; polymorphous rash; cervical lymphadenopathy. Ask the parent about features since the fever began, as some may have faded by the time you see the child.

The classic research definition is fever of 5 days or more with at least 4 of the 5 principal features (AHA 2017 [4], international). Incomplete Kawasaki has fewer. NG143 [1]: children under 1 year may present with fewer features but may be at higher risk of coronary artery abnormalities.

Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis and the commonest cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries [3]. Untreated, it can cause coronary artery aneurysms. Intravenous immunoglobulin with aspirin, given early (ideally within the first 10 days of illness), reduces that risk [3][4]. Diagnosis, echocardiography and treatment belong to the paediatric team.

BNFC: aspirin is not normally given to children under 16 because of Reye’s syndrome; Kawasaki disease is a recognised exception under specialist care. Parents must not start aspirin at home; doses and duration are set by the paediatric team.

Measles (coryza, cough, Koplik spots; check MMR status), scarlet fever (sore throat, sandpaper rash, responds to antibiotics), adenovirus and other viral exanthems, toxic shock, and drug reactions. None of these should delay a same-day paediatric assessment for a child with this cluster.

A video call can show the eyes, lips, rash and hands, but not the heart rate, capillary refill or hydration properly. NG143 [1] and NG254 [2] ask for a traffic-light and sepsis risk assessment; any red feature or high-risk sepsis criterion means emergency transfer. Otherwise phone the on-call paediatrician for same-day assessment.

NG143 [1]: antipyretics are for distress, not to bring the temperature down. Do not give paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time; consider alternating only if distress persists or recurs before the next dose is due. Encourage fluids. Doses per BNFC.

The mother’s sense of being dismissed; her support at home; practicalities of getting to hospital today.

Kawasaki disease versus measles, scarlet fever, viral exanthem, toxic shock, drug reaction.
NG143 traffic-light and NG254 sepsis features screened: responsiveness, breathing, hydration, non-blanching rash.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “six days”, “red eyes but not gunky”, “strawberry tongue” and “puffy red hands” as a pattern, not isolated symptoms.
Idea (something is wrong despite “just a virus”), concern (nobody listening, missing something serious), expectation (an answer and stronger fever treatment).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I feel something’s really wrong. She’s never been this poorly, and nobody’s listening." She fears she’ll be seen as a fussy mum — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Ahmed. Can you both hear and see me? … And you’re Ivy’s mum? Thanks for bringing her. Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Checks connection and relationship to the child; open question

model.text: I’m really worried about Ivy. She’s had a raging temperature for six days now. Calpol and Nurofen barely touch it. She’s got a blotchy rash, really red eyes but not gunky, cracked red lips, a tongue like a strawberry, and puffy red hands. She’s so miserable. Everyone says it’s just a virus, but six days?
Six days of high fever is a long time, and you’ve described some very specific things. You were right to call. I want to go through it carefully, because I’m not sure this is just a virus either.
model.why: Validates the mother’s concern early

model.text: Right now, how is she? Is she awake and responding to you, or very sleepy and hard to rouse?
model.why: NG143 traffic-light: activity and responsiveness first

model.text: She’s awake but grizzly and clingy. She just wants to be held.
Is she drinking, and how many wet nappies or wees today? Any vomiting?
model.why: Hydration screen

model.text: She’s drinking a bit, less than normal. Fewer wees than usual, I think.
Is her breathing fast or noisy? Any cough, runny nose or sore throat?
model.why: Respiratory red flags and measles or strep clues

model.text: No cough or runny nose. Her breathing seems okay.
Could you hold the camera close to the rash? … Now press a clear glass firmly on a spot. Does it fade?
model.why: Non-blanching rash check to exclude meningococcal disease

model.text: Yes, it goes pale under the glass.

Thank you. Now her eyes, lips and tongue, please … and her hands and feet. I can see the redness in both eyes without any discharge, dry cracked lips, and her palms look red and puffy. Is there a lump in her neck? Feel just under her jaw.
model.why: Uses video to look for the NG143 features

model.text: There’s a lump on this side. It’s tender, she pulls away.
When did each of these start? Some come and go, so tell me even if they’ve faded.
model.why: NG143: ask about features since fever onset

model.text: The fever first. The eyes and rash a couple of days later, then the lips, and her hands swelled up yesterday.
Has she been in contact with anyone with measles or a rash illness? Do you know if her jabs are up to date, including MMR?
model.why: Considers measles as the key mimic

model.text: Not that I know of. I think she’s up to date, but I’d need to check her red book.
Has she had any medicines other than Calpol and Nurofen, or any health problems before this?
model.why: Medication and past history for drug-reaction differential

model.text: No, just those.
You said everyone keeps calling it a virus. What have you been thinking yourself?
model.why: Explores the mother’s ideas

model.text: I just feel something’s wrong. She’s never been this poorly, and I feel like nobody’s listening.
I’m listening, and your instinct fits what I’m seeing. What were you hoping I’d do today?
model.why: Acknowledges feeling dismissed; asks expectations

model.text: Find out what it is. Something stronger for the fever, maybe.

Here’s what I think. A fever lasting more than five days, with red eyes without discharge, red cracked lips and a strawberry tongue, a rash, red swollen hands and a lump in the neck, fits a condition called Kawasaki disease. It’s an inflammation of the blood vessels, and it happens mostly in young children.
model.why: Names the likely diagnosis, linking each feature

model.text: I’ve never heard of it. Is it serious?

It can be, which is why I want to act today. It can affect the blood vessels that supply the heart. The good news is that treatment in hospital, usually a drip of immunoglobulin, works best when it starts early, and it greatly lowers that risk. We’re still within that window, so today matters.
model.why: Explains coronary risk and time-critical IVIG without alarming

model.text: Oh gosh. So she needs to go to hospital?

Yes. I’m going to phone the children’s doctors at the hospital as soon as we finish and ask them to see her this afternoon. They’ll examine her properly, do blood tests and a heart scan, and decide on treatment. I’ll tell them exactly what you’ve told me.
model.why: Same-day paediatric referral by phone with a clear handover

model.text: Can I drive her in myself?

She’s awake and her rash fades under the glass, so taking her in yourself is fine. If she becomes floppy, very hard to wake, is breathing fast or struggling, or goes pale or blotchy, call 999 instead.
model.why: Disposition matched to risk, with escalation criteria

model.text: Okay. What should I give her for the fever?

Keep giving Calpol or Nurofen only if she’s distressed, not just to bring the number down, and don’t give both at the same time. Sips of drink as often as she’ll take. Please don’t give her any aspirin yourself. Aspirin is only used in children by the hospital team, for this condition, under their supervision.
model.why: NG143 antipyretic advice; BNFC aspirin caution

model.text: I wouldn’t have known that.
And for you: you did exactly the right thing trusting your instinct. This isn’t overreacting. Is there anything that would make getting there this afternoon difficult?
model.why: Supports the parent and checks practicalities

model.text: No, I’ll sort it. I just want her seen.
Can you tell me back the plan, so I know I’ve explained it well?
model.why: Teach-back

model.text: You’re ringing the hospital now. I take her in this afternoon. Calpol or Nurofen only if she’s upset, not both together, no aspirin. 999 if she goes floppy, won’t wake or can’t breathe properly.
Perfect. I’ll ring you back within the next half hour to confirm where to go and who to ask for. If they’re expecting her sooner, I’ll let you know.
model.why: Closes the loop: callback, named destination, clear time frame

model.text: Thank you, doctor. Honestly, thank you for listening.

social.t: Parents repeatedly told “it’s a virus” may lose trust or stop seeking help. Taking the account seriously is safer and rebuilds confidence.
Employees have a statutory right to reasonable unpaid time off to deal with an emergency involving a dependant (Employment Rights Act 1996, time off for dependants).

legal.t: GMC 0–18 years guidance (2007): a person with parental responsibility can consent to examination and treatment for a young child; involve the child as far as her age allows.
GMC Good medical practice (2024): recognise the limits of a video assessment and arrange face-to-face care when the history suggests it is needed.

professional.t: Phone the on-call paediatrician rather than sending a letter; record the time of the call, what was said and the plan agreed.
A child seen several times for the same illness is a recognised risk for missed diagnosis. Consider a significant event review if earlier contacts missed the pattern.

community.t: Children treated for Kawasaki disease need hospital follow-up with repeat echocardiography; the GP may see her again for recovery, peeling skin and questions about vaccines after immunoglobulin (check the Green Book live-vaccine timing with the paediatric team).

redFlags: Fever of 5 days or more (NG143 amber)
Drowsy, floppy or hard to rouse
Reduced fluid intake and fewer wet nappies
Age under 1 with prolonged fever (fewer features, higher coronary risk)
psychosocial: Mother feels dismissed after several contacts
Support to get to hospital today
Her distress at seeing Ivy so miserable
ice: Idea: “something is wrong, it isn’t just a virus”
Concern: that nobody is listening and something serious is being missed
Expectation: an answer and something stronger for the fever

playbook.diagnosis: “Six days of fever with red eyes without discharge, red cracked lips, a strawberry tongue, a rash, puffy red hands and a neck gland fits Kawasaki disease, an inflammation of the blood vessels in young children.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The body’s defences are inflaming the walls of blood vessels. The vessels that feed the heart can be affected, which is why the hospital gives a treatment early to calm it down and checks her heart with a scan.”

management.reflectIce: “You felt something was wrong, and you were right. This needs more than stronger fever medicine; it needs the children’s team today.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the mother; check who can go with her; confirm she can get there safely; promise and make a callback.
sharedPlan: Phone the on-call paediatrician for same-day assessment; handover of fever duration and each feature
Hospital: bloods, echocardiography, IV immunoglobulin with aspirin if confirmed (specialist decision)
Antipyretics only for distress, not both together (NG143); fluids
safetyNet: 999 if floppy, very hard to wake, breathing fast or struggling, pale or mottled, or a rash that does not fade
Hospital follow-up and echocardiography after treatment

pitfalls.intro: The trap is joining the chorus of “just a virus”. The marks sit in noticing the fever duration, looking for the features on camera, and getting her seen by paediatrics today.

items.fail: Accepting the viral label without asking how long the fever has lasted.
items.why: NG143 asks you to think of Kawasaki disease at 5 days of fever.
items.fix: Ask the duration first and say out loud why it matters.

items.fail: Waiting for all 4 of 5 features before acting.
items.why: Incomplete Kawasaki is common and infants are at higher coronary risk; NG143 dropped the 4-feature requirement.
items.fix: Fever of 5 days plus any of the features means same-day paediatric review.

items.fail: No red-flag or sepsis screen on a video call.
items.why: NG143 and NG254 features decide between 999 and a same-day slot.
items.fix: Responsiveness, breathing, hydration and a glass test before the plan.

items.fail: Advising routine alternating antipyretics or suggesting aspirin.
items.why: NG143 says antipyretics are for distress; BNFC restricts aspirin in under-16s to specialist use.
items.fix: One antipyretic for distress; no aspirin at home.

items.why: Her concern is the hidden agenda and the reason she called.
items.fix: “You were right to push. Your instinct fits what I see.”

items.why: Vague advice and no handover leave the family to explain it all again.
items.fix: Phone the paediatrician, give specific 999 triggers, and call back with the plan.

Traffic-light features, hydration, glass test, then use the camera for eyes, lips, tongue, hands and neck. Timeline of each feature. Measles contacts and MMR.
Her instinct that something is wrong; feeling dismissed; what she hoped for.
Kawasaki disease; the heart vessel risk; why early treatment matters.
Phone the paediatric team; safe transport and 999 triggers; antipyretics for distress only, no aspirin; teach-back; callback.

wordPics.fail: Calls it a virus again and advises alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen; never asks how long the fever has lasted in relation to the other features; no same-day referral; no 999 advice.
wordPics.pass: Recognises that fever of 5 days or more with these features suggests Kawasaki disease, screens red flags, and arranges same-day paediatric assessment with clear safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: uses the video camera deliberately (glass test, eyes, lips, hands, neck); explains the coronary risk and the benefit of early immunoglobulin calmly; validates the mother’s instinct; phones the paediatrician directly; warns against home aspirin; teach-back and a timed callback.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably still a virus, give it another couple of days.”
avoid.instead: “Six days of fever with these changes needs the children’s team to see her today.”
avoid.why: Delay beyond the early treatment window increases the risk of coronary aneurysms.

avoid.dont: “Alternate Calpol and Nurofen every two hours to keep the temperature down.”
avoid.instead: “Give one of them if she’s distressed; don’t give both at once.”
avoid.why: NG143: antipyretics are for distress, not to lower the number; alternate only if distress persists.

avoid.dont: “She hasn’t got four of the five criteria yet, so it can’t be Kawasaki.”
avoid.instead: “She has a long fever with several features, and that’s enough to get her checked today.”
avoid.why: NG143 advises considering Kawasaki at 5 days of fever; incomplete disease is common, especially in infants.

It’s an inflammation of the blood vessels, and it happens mostly in young children.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the likely diagnosis, linking each feature

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ve never heard of it. Is it serious?

It can be, which is why I want to act today. It can affect the blood vessels that supply the heart. The good news is that treatment in hospital, usually a drip of immunoglobulin, works best when it starts early, and it greatly lowers that risk. We’re still within that window, so today matters.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains coronary risk and time-critical IVIG without alarming

SCA_MODELS.text: Oh gosh. So she needs to go to hospital?

Yes. I’m going to phone the children’s doctors at the hospital as soon as we finish and ask them to see her this afternoon. They’ll examine her properly, do blood tests and a heart scan, and decide on treatment. I’ll tell them exactly what you’ve told me.
SCA_MODELS.why: Same-day paediatric referral by phone with a clear handover

SCA_MODELS.text: Can I drive her in myself?

She’s awake and her rash fades under the glass, so taking her in yourself is fine. If she becomes floppy, very hard to wake, is breathing fast or struggling, or goes pale or blotchy, call 999 instead.
SCA_MODELS.why: Disposition matched to risk, with escalation criteria

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. What should I give her for the fever?

Keep giving Calpol or Nurofen only if she’s distressed, not just to bring the number down, and don’t give both at the same time. Sips of drink as often as she’ll take. Please don’t give her any aspirin yourself. Aspirin is only used in children by the hospital team, for this condition, under their supervision.
SCA_MODELS.why: NG143 antipyretic advice; BNFC aspirin caution

SCA_MODELS.text: I wouldn’t have known that.
And for you: you did exactly the right thing trusting your instinct. This isn’t overreacting. Is there anything that would make getting there this afternoon difficult?
SCA_MODELS.why: Supports the parent and checks practicalities

SCA_MODELS.text: No, I’ll sort it. I just want her seen.
Can you tell me back the plan, so I know I’ve explained it well?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: You’re ringing the hospital now. I take her in this afternoon. Calpol or Nurofen only if she’s upset, not both together, no aspirin. 999 if she goes floppy, won’t wake or can’t breathe properly.
Perfect. I’ll ring you back within the next half hour to confirm where to go and who to ask for. If they’re expecting her sooner, I’ll let you know.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes the loop: callback, named destination, clear time frame

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you, doctor. Honestly, thank you for listening.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG143 (Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management, 2019) · [2] NICE NG254 (Suspected sepsis in under 16s) · [3] Eleftheriou et al., Management of Kawasaki disease, Arch Dis Child 2014;99:74–83 (UK) · [4] American Heart Association scientific statement on Kawasaki disease (McCrindle et al., Circulation 2017, international)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Fever lasting five days or more in a young child should make you think of Kawasaki disease. Ivy has the fever plus conjunctival injection, lip and tongue changes, a rash, hand changes and a neck node. She needs the paediatric team today, because early immunoglobulin treatment reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysms.

points.h: Think of it at five days
points.t: NICE NG143 [1]: be aware of the possibility of Kawasaki disease in children with fever that has lasted 5 days or longer. Fever of 5 days or more is also an amber feature in the NG143 traffic-light table. Since 2019 NG143 no longer requires 4 of the 5 principal features before you consider it, because early and incomplete cases often show fewer.

NG143 [1] lists: bilateral conjunctival injection without exudate; erythema and cracking of the lips, strawberry tongue or erythema of the oral and pharyngeal mucosa; oedema and erythema of the hands or feet; polymorphous rash; cervical lymphadenopathy. Ask the parent about features since the fever began, as some may have faded by the time you see the child.

The classic research definition is fever of 5 days or more with at least 4 of the 5 principal features (AHA 2017 [4], international). Incomplete Kawasaki has fewer. NG143 [1]: children under 1 year may present with fewer features but may be at higher risk of coronary artery abnormalities.

Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis and the commonest cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries [3]. Untreated, it can cause coronary artery aneurysms. Intravenous immunoglobulin with aspirin, given early (ideally within the first 10 days of illness), reduces that risk [3][4]. Diagnosis, echocardiography and treatment belong to the paediatric team.

BNFC: aspirin is not normally given to children under 16 because of Reye’s syndrome; Kawasaki disease is a recognised exception under specialist care. Parents must not start aspirin at home; doses and duration are set by the paediatric team.

Measles (coryza, cough, Koplik spots; check MMR status), scarlet fever (sore throat, sandpaper rash, responds to antibiotics), adenovirus and other viral exanthems, toxic shock, and drug reactions. None of these should delay a same-day paediatric assessment for a child with this cluster.

A video call can show the eyes, lips, rash and hands, but not the heart rate, capillary refill or hydration properly. NG143 [1] and NG254 [2] ask for a traffic-light and sepsis risk assessment; any red feature or high-risk sepsis criterion means emergency transfer. Otherwise phone the on-call paediatrician for same-day assessment.

NG143 [1]: antipyretics are for distress, not to bring the temperature down. Do not give paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time; consider alternating only if distress persists or recurs before the next dose is due. Encourage fluids. Doses per BNFC.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let the mother tell the whole story; confirmed who was on the call and that both could be seen and heard.
The mother’s sense of being dismissed; her support at home; practicalities of getting to hospital today.
Picked up “six days”, “red eyes but not gunky”, “strawberry tongue” and “puffy red hands” as a pattern, not isolated symptoms.
Idea (something is wrong despite “just a virus”), concern (nobody listening, missing something serious), expectation (an answer and stronger fever treatment).
Used the camera for eyes, lips, tongue, hands, rash (glass test) and neck; recognised that observations need a face-to-face paediatric assessment.
Kawasaki disease versus measles, scarlet fever, viral exanthem, toxic shock, drug reaction.
NG143 traffic-light and NG254 sepsis features screened: responsiveness, breathing, hydration, non-blanching rash.
Probable Kawasaki disease: fever 5 days or more with the NG143 features.
Same-day paediatric assessment arranged by phone; explained IVIG and echocardiography; no aspirin at home; antipyretics for distress only.
Checked for barriers to getting there today; acknowledged the mother’s distress; transport safe given current state.
999 triggers named; callback within 30 minutes with destination; teach-back confirmed.

social.t: Parents repeatedly told “it’s a virus” may lose trust or stop seeking help. Taking the account seriously is safer and rebuilds confidence.
Employees have a statutory right to reasonable unpaid time off to deal with an emergency involving a dependant (Employment Rights Act 1996, time off for dependants).

legal.t: GMC 0–18 years guidance (2007): a person with parental responsibility can consent to examination and treatment for a young child; involve the child as far as her age allows.
GMC Good medical practice (2024): recognise the limits of a video assessment and arrange face-to-face care when the history suggests it is needed.

professional.t: Phone the on-call paediatrician rather than sending a letter; record the time of the call, what was said and the plan agreed.
A child seen several times for the same illness is a recognised risk for missed diagnosis. Consider a significant event review if earlier contacts missed the pattern.

community.t: Children treated for Kawasaki disease need hospital follow-up with repeat echocardiography; the GP may see her again for recovery, peeling skin and questions about vaccines after immunoglobulin (check the Green Book live-vaccine timing with the paediatric team).

redFlags: Fever of 5 days or more (NG143 amber)
Drowsy, floppy or hard to rouse
Reduced fluid intake and fewer wet nappies
Age under 1 with prolonged fever (fewer features, higher coronary risk)
psychosocial: Mother feels dismissed after several contacts
Support to get to hospital today
Her distress at seeing Ivy so miserable
ice: Idea: “something is wrong, it isn’t just a virus”
Concern: that nobody is listening and something serious is being missed
Expectation: an answer and something stronger for the fever

management.psychosocial: Validate the mother; check who can go with her; confirm she can get there safely; promise and make a callback.
sharedPlan: Phone the on-call paediatrician for same-day assessment; handover of fever duration and each feature
Hospital: bloods, echocardiography, IV immunoglobulin with aspirin if confirmed (specialist decision)
Antipyretics only for distress, not both together (NG143); fluids
safetyNet: 999 if floppy, very hard to wake, breathing fast or struggling, pale or mottled, or a rash that does not fade
Hospital follow-up and echocardiography after treatment

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is joining the chorus of “just a virus”. The marks sit in noticing the fever duration, looking for the features on camera, and getting her seen by paediatrics today.

items.fail: Accepting the viral label without asking how long the fever has lasted.
items.why: NG143 asks you to think of Kawasaki disease at 5 days of fever.
items.fix: Ask the duration first and say out loud why it matters.

items.fail: Waiting for all 4 of 5 features before acting.
items.why: Incomplete Kawasaki is common and infants are at higher coronary risk; NG143 dropped the 4-feature requirement.
items.fix: Fever of 5 days plus any of the features means same-day paediatric review.

items.fail: No red-flag or sepsis screen on a video call.
items.why: NG143 and NG254 features decide between 999 and a same-day slot.
items.fix: Responsiveness, breathing, hydration and a glass test before the plan.

items.fail: Advising routine alternating antipyretics or suggesting aspirin.
items.why: NG143 says antipyretics are for distress; BNFC restricts aspirin in under-16s to specialist use.
items.fix: One antipyretic for distress; no aspirin at home.

items.why: Her concern is the hidden agenda and the reason she called.
items.fix: “You were right to push. Your instinct fits what I see.”

items.why: Vague advice and no handover leave the family to explain it all again.
items.fix: Phone the paediatrician, give specific 999 triggers, and call back with the plan.
